prize_parts.citation: for showing how technological change and trade shocks reshape labour demand, wages and local labour markets

statement.case_for: B023 rests on conceptually clear and empirically credible work. The task-based and skill-biased accounts of technology, together with the import-competition evidence, changed how economists and policymakers understand wage inequality, polarisation and the adjustment costs borne by local labour markets. The work has been replicated and criticised for one to three decades. It was also the only candidate ranked by all eleven members in the opening round, which is a sign of breadth across fields but not of merit. On the substance, the research designs (quasi-experimental variation, administrative and local-market data) are the kind that have raised credibility standards in applied economics. The main findings have survived years of scrutiny, even though magnitudes are still debated. A three-name award can be framed around one question: how technology and trade change the demand for labour. Autor is central to both strands. Katz anchors the earlier skill-biased technical change and wage-structure evidence. Hanson is central to the trade-shock evidence.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that B023 bundles two discoveries, the technology-and-skills line and the China-shock line. The credit is therefore split, and a three-name cap forces a hard choice. Dorn is a core co-author of the China-shock papers and is left out. Katz's strand partly overlaps with work that other laureates are associated with. The size and persistence of the trade-shock effects, and the shift-share identification behind them, remain contested. If the Committee prefers a single, sharply bounded discovery, B006 (Kiyotaki-Moore) or B047 (BLP) may be cleaner.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranked B023 lower and proposed Autor, Hanson and Dorn. She sees Katz's work as overlapping with an earlier recognition (Goldin), and she finds the discovery less unified because trade shocks and technology are distinct strands.
responses.response: I take the unity concern seriously, but I do not find the overlap with Goldin decisive. The 2023 prize was for women's labour-market outcomes, and Katz's skill-premium and wage-structure work with Murphy is a different body of evidence. I agree that Autor-Dorn-Hanson is the tightest attribution for the trade-shock papers, and Dorn's exclusion is a real cost of my configuration. I keep Katz because the prize would then cover the technology and wage-structure evidence on which the trade-shock literature builds, and I frame the citation around labour demand to hold the two strands together. I would not oppose a committee that preferred the Dorn variant.

responses.point: Hassler ranked B006 first with Kiyotaki and Moore only. He argues that Gertler's accelerator work builds on Bernanke-Gertler and that Bernanke's 2022 prize already recognises the financial-crisis side, so a two-person award is the cleanest attribution.
responses.response: I partly concede this. My opening proposal included Gertler, but the accelerator credit is shared with an existing laureate, and a Kiyotaki-Moore pair is the more defensible B006 configuration. That strengthens B006 as a competitor, and it is why I list it as an alternative. I still rank B023 first for two reasons. The B023 empirical evidence is broader in reach, and in labour and trade it has been tested more directly against data and policy. In B006, empirical identification of the collateral channel is mixed, as Hassler and others note. This is a judgement on relative strength, not a claim that B006 is weak.

responses.point: Boppart ranked B023 first. He regards Dorn as arguably equally deserving and flags that identification in the shift-share designs has been debated. He also notes the partial overlap of Katz's work with an earlier prize.
responses.response: I agree on all three points, and I do not think they are resolved by the cap on names. I would add that the shift-share debate affects the magnitude and mechanism of the China-shock estimates more than the core qualitative finding. I rely on recall for that and have not checked the literature. For that reason I put more weight on the task and wage-structure evidence and on the persistence of local adjustment costs than on any single point estimate. I also see Dorn's omission as the main weakness of my configuration, and I would welcome the Committee's view on whether a Dorn-for-Katz swap is warranted.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee treats technology and trade as one coherent discovery or as two, and whether the third name should be Katz or Dorn.
How persistent and how large the local effects of import competition are, and how robust the shift-share identification is. I rely on recall, not source checking.
Whether B006, which had the strongest opening support, is better judged without Gertler given the Bernanke overlap, and whether it would then be preferred to B023.
How much weight to give B023's broad support across fields, since support counts are not scientific merit.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for the B023 candidates: the profile lists no co-authorship or institutional tie to Autor, Hanson, Katz or Dorn. My research is in empirical labour economics, which is close to the topic, and I have tried to apply the common criteria. I overlapped institutionally with Hassler and Krusell at Stockholm University (2010-17), which is not a co-authorship.
